segments.text: “Hey friends, do you know who the most powerful person in the
world was two thousand years ago?
Well, at that time, the most powerful empire in the world was the Roman Empire,
and the emperor of Rome was considered the most powerful person in the world.
Why? Because kings usually rule over a kingdom — they usually have one
country or one kingdom.” “But an emperor rules over many kingdoms.
Many kings usually come under him.
That’s why an emperor is extremely powerful.
Especially this emperor, whose name is Marcus Aurelius — you may have heard
of him — is considered one of the greatest emperors in all of history because
he faced many problems in his life.” “He fought many wars, witnessed floods
in his kingdom, faced a pandemic, and even experienced betrayals and deception.
Along with all this, he saw the death of his eight children.
Yet despite everything,
he remained calm, made wise decisions, and always stood strong like a true leader.
Because of all these qualities, people respect him greatly.
In fact, it is said that after him, no emperor like him ever came again.”
“But the question is: what was so special about him?
What was the thing that made him so powerful?
He had a secret habit —
a habit that you, too, can practice daily for just one minute.
And by doing so, you can develop the same mental resilience, strength,
and leadership qualities within yourself.
The habit that made Marcus Aurelius so mentally strong was the habit
of journaling — writing.” “No matter how busy he was — whether he was
heading to wars
or dealing with any kind of difficulty — he always made time for journaling.
It means he would write his thoughts and ideas on paper.
He had created his own private notebook, and the sole purpose of that notebook
was to put down whatever was on his mind onto paper.” “Many
times, he would understand his own ego, anger, and fears by writing them down.
He didn’t create
this book to publish it, but you know what interesting thing happened?
The notes he had written only for himself were later turned into a book almost two
thousand years later, called Meditations, which is considered
one of the most powerful self-help books of all time.”
“Bill Clinton, Tim Ferriss, Steve Jobs, Naval Ravikant, and many other powerful
leaders even today learn from
Marcus Aurelius’s book and his teachings to become better and stronger leaders.
And if you also want to become a strong leader, then today I’m not just going
to tell you about a book — I’m going to share a system, a simple system that
can help you reset and rewire your
mind.” “And that too by practicing this daily habit for just one minute.
What is the neuroscience behind it?
How is this scientifically possible?
Then I’m going to share not five, not six, but seven
methods that will help you journal in just one minute.
What to journal, how to write — I’ll explain all of that to you
through these techniques.” “Plus, practice number six is my personal favorite —
the one I’ve been doing the most, and I’ve been following it for many years.
I’ll share that journaling method with you in the 6th technique.
And at the end of this video, I’m going to share three powerful
books that will genuinely help you apply
this journaling habit practically.” “So now let’s start with the science.
People who write for just one minute every morning are happier and
achieve more throughout their day — and this is proven by science.
Do you know why?
Whenever you write, your prefrontal cortex — which is very important for focus,
clarity, and decision-making — gets activated, it lights up.” “On the other
hand, your amygdala — which is responsible for fear and stress — starts
to calm down.
The moment you begin writing, even your reticular activating system
gets activated.
Whatever you write, your focus shifts toward it, and your attention naturally
increases in that direction.” “In fact, let’s leave the theory aside.
I want you to go and do something practical right now.
Go, take a pen and paper, and start writing your goals on it.
What do you want in life?
What is it that you want to stay as the focus of your life?
Because remember, wherever your focus goes, your energy goes — and wherever your
energy goes, that’s where you will get results.” “So before learning all
the techniques, go and do this one thing right now if you want — write a little.
Write your goals.
And if you don’t have a pen and paper, then write your
goals in the comments — the ones you want to achieve.
And in simple language, this itself can be called journaling.
Look, journaling doesn’t
mean you have to write long messages, stories, or poems.”
“If you write even your small goals, if you take the things in your mind
and put them down on pen and paper, that too is considered a form of journaling.
And I’m not the one saying this — Ryan Holiday, the author of The Daily Stoic,
The Obstacle Is the Way, and many other powerful books,
has explained many such things in The Daily Stoic Journal.”
“From that same book, I’m going to tell you five things
today that will help you journal in the best possible way.
So let’s move to those methods — those techniques that can help you
journal effectively. The first one is The Control One.
Do you know,
in 2008, Starbucks was in very bad shape?” “The stock price was falling.
The company had become almost bankrupt and was on the verge of shutting down.
At that time, Howard Schultz decided that he would return as the
CEO, and he took full control back into his own hands.
Every morning, he started asking himself a question and began writing about it.
What was that question?
The question was: What is in my control today?” “When he wrote about
this, he realized that he couldn’t change the economy, he couldn’t change the
government, and he couldn’t change people.
But there were definitely some things within his control that he could change —
like how good the
coffee would be, how excellent they could make it, the training of the
staff, the trust he had in his employees, and the trust others had in him.
And to rebuild all of this…” “After getting this clarity, he decided
to shut down all 7,000 of their stores for a day.
Because of this, the company lost millions and millions of dollars.
People said he had made a crazy move.
But that one move, you could say, rewired the entire company.
Two years later, because of this rewiring, Starbucks’ sales had tripled.” “Their
valuation tripled.
And all of this happened because instead of focusing on the things that
were not in his control, he focused on the things that were in his control.
Let’s take another beautiful example — an Indian example. Dr.
A.P.J.
Abdul Kalam.
When he built his first SLV rocket and launched it,
it failed.” “This was in 1979.
He was obviously disappointed.
But he didn’t blame the weather, the government, or anyone else.
That night, when he went home, he simply journaled and wrote: I can’t
control the outcome, but I can control the preparation for the next launch.
The outcome wasn’t in his hands, but the hard work was — and he spent
the next year focusing only on what was in his control.” “And guess what?
Within just one year, India
launched its first satellite successfully and created history across the world.
Even during World War II, Viktor Frankl did something similar.
When he was imprisoned in a Nazi camp, when he lost his parents, his wife —
he had lost everything — even then, he chose to focus on the one thing that
was still in his control.” “Torture from others, not being given food —
none of that was in his control.
But he understood one thing: everything
can be taken from you except your power to choose your attitude.
He would note this down mentally.
Many thoughts would come to his mind,
and he would scrape them together, understand them, and reflect on them.
He didn’t even have pen and paper.” “He would express his ideas in whatever small
ways he could, capturing them mentally, and once he was freed, he turned all those
ideas into a book — Man’s Search for Meaning — which became one of the
greatest self-help books of all time.
That’s why you too can use this in your one-minute journaling.
What do you have to do?” “Start writing for just one minute.
Whatever is bothering you
right now, giving you tension or stress — go and write it down.
And then apply this simple
formula: whatever is bothering you, ask yourself — Is this in my control?
Only two answers will come out: either yes or no.”
“If the answer is yes, then think about how you can take action and fix it.
Can you do something or not? If yes, great.
If not, then there’s no need to take tension. If the answer is no, and
you can’t do anything about it, then it’s okay — you’ll have to let it go.
Start doing this simple exercise, and
the moment you take these thoughts out of your mind and put them onto paper…”
“You will feel a sense of calm when you write it down.
You’ll feel good.
Just do it for one minute and see its magic. Next is The Gratitude One.
Did you know Dr.
Robert Emmons conducted research at
UC Davis where he divided people into two groups?
He told one group that every night before sleeping, they had to write down three
things they were grateful for.” “The things that make you feel good — and the
second group was told to write about things they complained about or didn’t
like. And guess what happened?
The group that practiced gratitude saw their happiness increase by 25%.
They started sleeping better.
They started
going to the gym more, exercising more…” “They even started doing it consistently.
In fact, their overall doctor visits even reduced — all because of this one
habit of writing three things they were grateful for before sleeping. Science
shows that gratitude literally rewires your brain to look for good things.
That’s why even if you do this exercise for just one or two minutes, it will
give you tremendous
results.” “Reports say that Ratan Tata often wrote gratitude notes — not because
he was very wealthy, and not for his wealth — but for the people in his life.
He once said, ‘The day I forget the people who helped me rise is the day
I start falling.’ This shows where his focus was — not on money, but on people.
And maybe that’s why people still admire him so much today.” “Kathleen Kogan, who
is a Russian-born American entrepreneur,
author, and emotional-fitness expert, says that when she
started her startup, she used to feel a lot of burnout and stress.
So she took up a 21-day challenge — 21 Days to Be More Happy and Less
Stressed. When she did this challenge, she noticed how her mood started improving
and how she was able to work on her startup in a much better way.”
“That’s why you should simply take out one minute a day — before
sleeping or whenever you get time — and write three things you are grateful for.
I would even say, do it right now if you want.
Go to the chat and write them. If more than three things come to your mind,
write more —
things you’re grateful for, maybe the internet, videos, your home, water, food…”
“There are so many things you can feel grateful for — if you want, write
them right now in the comments, and I’ll read them. Next is The Awareness One.
Has it ever happened that one of your friends
got into a fight, and after the fight he sat there feeling very stressed?
You can see that he’s taking a lot of stress, right?”
“You go and explain to him, ‘It’s okay, the fight happened.
It’s fine, it will get better in some time —
maybe by tomorrow, the day after, or even in a month. Don’t stress.
What will stressing do?’ But no matter
how much you explain, he doesn’t understand, right?
He still keeps stressing. Now notice the opposite — many
times the same thing happens to us too, when we get into a fight.”
“Our mood becomes completely upset.
Someone else comes and tries to explain
things to us, but we still don’t understand. Why does that happen?
Well, the reason is association and dissociation.
Many times, when we are personally going
through a problem, we are associated with it.
But if we learn to dissociate ourselves from that problem — the way a friend would
— then we step away from the problem and look at it from a
dissociated perspective.” “That’s why it doesn’t even seem like such a big issue.
Many times it feels like things will eventually get better,
but when we ourselves
are stuck deep inside the problem, we feel as if nothing can be fixed anymore.
Right? There’s a very effective way to deal with this too: journaling.
After the England series in 2014, when Virat Kohli was going through
the worst phase of his cricket career, he started journaling.” “About his anger
and his ego—and he realized that he had stopped enjoying the game.
And this self-awareness is what led him toward meditation
and discipline, eventually making him one of the greatest players.
Socrates said, ‘The unexamined life is not worth living.’ Whenever you write, many
times what happens is that you, as I explained earlier,
naturally start to disassociate yourself.”
“When you disassociate, your self-awareness increases.
You start noticing your own patterns—your good habits, your triggers,
your fears, your behaviors—and all of these things raise your awareness.
And the more self-aware a person is, the better decisions they can make and
the better they can perform.” “That’s why you should start doing this
for just one minute.
Start writing for
one minute—about yourself, your fears, your triggers, your habits, your problems.
When you start writing them down, you will be able to disassociate yourself and
see what’s actually happening.
This will give your brain clarity.
Now let’s move to the next one — the fourth one, the preparation one.
Before every race, Michael Phelps — who you can say is...” “One of the
world’s greatest Olympic athletes, who has won around 26 Olympic medals.
You know this — before every race, he used to do mental rehearsal.
Stroke by stroke, he would run a visualization movie in his mind.
He even visualized a scenario where his goggles might break, fill with water,
he might get a cramp, or he might get a bad start — and you know what, something
like that actually happened.” “In the 2008 Beijing Olympics, when he started
his race, water entered his goggles.
And because he had
practiced that situation so many times in his mind, he didn’t panic.
He closed his eyes and swam without being able to see properly.
And guess what — even with that issue, he still won the gold medal.”
“His coach says that Michael Phelps has swum hundreds of times in his mind.
Michael Phelps had already prepared himself in advance.
Marcus Aurelius used to do something similar.
Every morning, he would remind himself—often by writing it down—‘Today
I will meet the selfish, the angry, the jealous.’ Basically, he would
write this.” “He knew that the day might not be perfect.
Not everything would go well—there could be some problems.
But whatever the problem was, he would handle it.
And this is the power of journaling.
It creates emotional armor for you.
Especially if you also write about what could go wrong, what the
worst-case scenario might be.” “How will you handle it?
Basically, preparing for the worst and hoping for the best.
This is something journaling will help you with a lot.
If you spend even one minute writing about what could go wrong, how you will handle
it, and what you need to do for the best-case scenario—writing
about these three things will make you very powerful.”
“Next, the fifth one — the reflection one.
Did you know that when Benjamin Franklin was 20 years old, he created
a tiny notebook in which he wrote down thirteen virtues?
These were qualities a person should have, such as humanity, humility,
having a good temper, not getting angry, and so on.
He wrote about thirteen different virtues in this way.” “And what he used to
do was judge himself every night before going to bed — how much humility he showed
that day, how much he learned, how well he managed his temper and emotions.
He treated this like a ritual and followed it for many years.
Because of this one habit, he went from being a broke apprentice…” “…into
one of history’s greatest inventors, diplomats, and self-made millionaires.
That’s why this habit
is also incredibly powerful — even if you do it for just one minute.
But every night before sleeping, reflect on how your day went.
What went well today, what went wrong, where you did well, and where you didn’t.
What did I do well today?
What can I do better tomorrow?” “Even if you write just these two things
in one minute, it will help you tremendously — by reflecting on yourself
and moving toward growth. Next is my favourite one — the random one.
Ryan Holiday also talks about this.
See, many times when you sit down to journal, you start overthinking.
What should I write? How should I write?
Rules, regulations… all sorts of things.
And because you get stuck thinking about all this, you never actually start.”
“That’s why this is the best method for everyone.
Start writing whatever random thoughts are coming to your mind.
As you can see, there are so many such pages.
You know, I have so many diaries filled up like this.
Different pages — I haven’t even made a proper journal.
Many times, each page just has random writing on it.
Whatever thoughts
come to me, I write them down.” “Whenever any idea comes, I write it down.
If something was discussed in a meeting, I write that down too.
Many times ideas keep coming into the mind like this.
And what do I do with all those ideas?
When I start getting too confused, I begin writing them down. Randomly.
And when I write whatever is going on in my mind, I notice something.”
“Automatically, my mind feels lighter.
I gain more clarity.
I understand better what I should do and what I shouldn’t.
That’s why this one — the random one — is my favorite.
Don’t overthink; just start writing whatever comes to your mind.
Keep the friction low.
You don’t need too many rules or regulations.”
“Whenever you get even one minute, just write.
Right now, write down any idea that comes to mind.
This is also a habit of billionaires.
Many times when ideas come to them, they take pen and paper and write
them down somewhere — because they never know which idea might come in handy later.
So note it down.
Our brain, you see, is not made to store memory.”
“The brain is made to create ideas, and a lot of them.
If you try to store everything in your memory, there will be problems.
That’s why don’t try to remember too much.
Just write down the ideas as they come. And finally, I want you
to comment and tell me — there are many ways to do journaling.
I know many of you are already journaling, so tell us in the comments how you
do it, so that others can read and learn from it too.” “I myself will also
read your comments, and I’ll even pin the best ones — the journaling methods that
worked for you — so that others can benefit, and you can help others as well.
You can write that down below.
Look, if you’ve reached this far in the video, it means you’re a serious person.
And I want you, since you are this serious, to take this seriousness
to the next level.” “Most people, you see, start a video but don’t even finish it.
If you’ve watched this video till the end, it means you have the drive
to take things to the next level — and that’s where the real game happens.
Go deeper into journaling.
Don’t just learn about it; actually make it a habit.
And to help you do this, three books will be very useful.” “One book is The
Miracle Morning, another is Atomic Habits, and the third is The Power of Habit.
I think you should read all three.
If you truly want to bring the habit of journaling into your life and implement
it, no matter how much theory you learn, you won’t get results until
you do it practically.
And to practice it, you need to take one step further and learn things
in depth.” “You’ll need to give more energy
and focus to get results, and that’s why you should read these books.
But I know, to read these big books, you’ll need to find time, buy them, and
put in the energy and effort.
If you can’t give that much energy
and effort, here’s the best second alternative.
I’ve created it for you all.
What we did is, my team and I read these books completely, chapter by chapter…”
“We took the very best points from these books and summarized them chapter
by chapter, highlighting all the
key takeaways so that you could get all the good insights clearly.
We also created detailed summaries.
And I knew that even reading the summaries might bore you or you might not be able
to read them, so we took it one step further and had it recorded.”
“With a professional voice-over artist.
And I knew what would happen now — you could listen to it anytime, anywhere.
Like me, I also like to listen while traveling.
You can listen to books anyway, but we didn’t stop there.
We went one step further, invested more, and created animations so that, just
like you enjoy watching videos, you can go through this entire book as a
web-series–style video.”
“So, to do this, we spent millions of rupees, to be honest.
Fifty thousand, one lakh, two lakh — all of this was spent to create each book.
Creating such video-books, which we have also sold for thousands of rupees.
But now, you know,
we have made the complete video-book of The Miracle Morning and the other
three books I mentioned, and it’s ready for you.” “Although it cost us millions
of rupees to create these books, you know, for now we’ve set a special price.
You could call it a very special experiment.
Just for now, for ₹99 per month, you get these three books,
and on top of that, not 10, not 20, but over
60 other carefully selected, best-in-class books that I have chosen.”
“You’ll get access to all the
video-books we’ve created for just ₹99 per month.
So that’s the deal with all these books.
You can invest just ₹99 to learn and implement them.
These books are very good for building the habit of journaling.
You must listen to them and watch the video-books.
The link is given below.
And a special thing — anyone who joins through the link below will
get special entry into my book club, again completely free of cost.” “But the
good thing is, in that book club, we won’t just learn about the books.
We’ll also discuss how to implement them.
I will personally share how I implement journaling, some special insights
that I haven’t shared here, directly with you live on Zoom.
And yes, I plan to do this Zoom session every month, and I will do it especially
for those who are joining now by paying just ₹99 — only ₹99.” “For them too, I
will hold a live session.
We’ll meet live on Zoom, discuss things related to journaling, share ideas,
and create a book club.
And we won’t make it a small, ordinary book club — we are going to build
the biggest book club in the world, and I need your support in it.
Make sure to join for just ₹99.
We’ll meet in the live class where we’ll discuss this book and journaling together.
Alright, that’s it for today. See you in the next video. Bye-bye!”
